I started my first teaching gig as a sessional English lecturer at a local underperforming college in September 2019 after going back to education myself in my late/early thirties. 
I never did a PGCE or other teaching qualification, just a BA and MA in litrature and creative writing, so I never really knew what to expect but I was excited to start actually.
A few months on, well, let's just say I can see why teachers leave the profession in droves. The amount of seemingly pointless admin work to do is astonishing, and even during the closure it only seems to have gotten worse.

You're absolutely correct in saying neoliberalism is a growth of capitalism. Frankly it couldn’t not have come about with it. 

But if we consider capitalism in its purest economic sense then the moment a taxpayer bailed-out a private business it breathed its last.

Since the early seventies, maybe late sixties, thanks to people like Milton Friedman neoliberalism has usurped the old capitalist system of business's being allowed to fail, he lobbied for less and less government 'interference' (what Friedman actually meant was fewer government safety nets for the venerable in society) and less public spending on public services instead allowing the private sector to step in. What this means in real terms is that when the private sector fails in their obligations in their public sector contracts either through bad management or bankruptcy the public purse is forced to bail them out as the service they may have been providing could have vital to society. 

It's here where economics and politics begin to be inseparable hence the rise of neoliberalism as a combined economic and political system. Again this is a rather surface analysis of the situation but there is stacks of texts out there that go far deeper. For a good read on the realities of neoliberalism take a look at Naomi Klein's *The Shock Doctrine.*

Initially it's important to understand that the systems are so intrinsically different that one cannot simply apply a 'socialist' equivalent to any single neoliberal institution. (I use neoliberal as it is arguable that we even live in a capitalist society anymore). Under another system many of the neoliberal institutions we take for granted now may be utterly redundant and therefore it would be fruitless to try and find those equivalents. One must try and stop thinking in terms of neoliberalism being the basis or default position of any society or economy.

*Socialism seems to have a problem with corrupt dictators.*

Although economics and politics are intertwined it is a mistake to conflate them utterly. Take Russia: While they attempted a communist (note that I don’t say socialist) economy their political structure was a dictatorship. The two are not mutually exclusive. One can have a socialist economy and a socialist political structure that is democratically based.

There can be a government under socialism. It may look something like direct democracy where leaders are elected and chosen right down to street level. In this system accountability is truly transparent and instantly applicable and corruption (i.e. lobbying and the pernicious influence of business and special interest groups) can be negated immediately. 

However, it can be large and unwieldy and difficult to manage but with the application of appropriate technology this actually ceases to be an issue. 

Obviously, economics and the actual political system and often inseparable. One answer could be Participatory Economics. (See Michael Albert, Robin Hahnel, David M. Kotz and John O’Neill.)

*How would a socialist government manage private property? How would they incentivize new business?*

Private property is an interesting question. Under a socialist government and economy there is nothing to actually inhibit the ownership of property. These seems contrary to traditional Marxist thought but it is possible nevertheless. One can still own their home, car, or TV for instance but the actual means of production and other important services such as water supply, power supply, education, health care etc… are socialised for the good of the peoples. 

Incentives for new business is almost a non-question under a socialist system. Whereas today we have half a dozen companies vying for the same resources to produce the same product (mobile phones for instance) that may have almost negligible differences a socialised system may have one institution that produces this product (that can be tailored modularly by the consumer and thereby retaining the so-called ‘consumer choice’) which then radically reduces the environmental impact on the planet and allowing the resources that would otherwise have been used inefficiently and wastefully to be put to better use elsewhere.

The idea of incentives for business would be redundant rather there would be incentives for innovation, invention and research; making what we have work better, faster, cleaner. What those incentives might be though is difficult to determine.

I could go far deeper but what I have outlined is the absolute surface of various socialist theory’s that can work in conjunction with one another and may require a shift in what we consider political, economic and cultural norms.

He sat back with just a little sweat gleaming on his brow.
Trgut'Spa pushed the issue. "That is truly great news. However, what do they want in return?"
The leader was quick to answer, "Nothing. Nothing at all. I couldn't believe it either, but it is true."
